title: How Currency Works
summary: Josh and Chuck open with childhood collecting memories (coin dispensers, banks, Mad magazine, Sports Illustrated), then use the Tide laundry detergent black market as a jumping-off point to explain currency. They cover the functions of currency (making change, storing wealth, medium of exchange), the four categories (commodity, coins, paper money, electronic), early examples like cacao beans, cattle and goats, Lydian and Chinese coins, Roman currency debasement, Swedish and goldsmith paper money, the gold standard and the Wizard of Oz allegory, fiat currency and perception of value, the Big Mac Index, inflation and deflation, Weimar Germany hyperinflation and the Rentenmark, large-denomination bills like the $100,000 bill, credit cards and electronic money, cowrie shells, etymology of words like buck, fee, dollar, salary and simoleon, and a listener mail shout-out to Bree Bagnal.
topics: Wizard of Oz gold standard allegory

segments.title: Opening banter and childhood collections
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck trade memories of collecting coin dispensers, piggy banks, Mad magazine, baseball cards and Sports Illustrated.

segments.title: Tide black market and currency defined
segments.summary: The hosts discuss a New York Magazine article on liquid Tide being stolen and used as a currency for buying drugs, and define currency as an agreed-upon medium of exchange.

segments.title: Why currency arose: making change and storing wealth
segments.summary: Currency solved barter problems by allowing change to be made and letting people store wealth instead of perishable goods like corn, which helped rise the merchant class.

segments.title: Four categories of currency and commodity money
segments.summary: The hosts outline commodity currency, coins, paper money and electronic currency, using cacao beans of the Aztecs and cattle and goats as examples of commodity money and its drawbacks.

segments.title: Early coins: Lydia, Rome, and China
segments.summary: Coins were first minted in Lydia under King Croesus around 600 BC and were adopted by Greece and Rome; early Chinese money took the form of tools and later round coins with holes. Roman emperors debased coinage, contributing to the empire's decline.

segments.title: Paper money, goldsmith notes, and the gold standard
segments.summary: Paper money began in China, failed in Sweden in 1661 due to oversupply, and caught on in the eighteenth century from goldsmith IOUs. Money was gold-backed in the US until 1933-era abandonment; the hosts mention the Wizard of Oz as a gold standard allegory.

segments.title: Electronic money, large bills, and credit cards
segments.summary: Electronic money grew after World War Two as banks settled through magnetic tape at the Federal Reserve. Large-denomination bills such as the $100,000 bill were used between banks. Diners Club introduced the first credit card, and direct deposit and electronic transfers followed.

segments.title: Perception of value, Big Mac Index, and inflation
segments.summary: Currency value depends on public belief; devaluation to attract investment is discussed, and the Big Mac Index is described as a tongue-in-cheek way to compare purchasing power. Supply and demand drive inflation and deflation.

segments.title: Weimar Germany hyperinflation and cowrie shells
segments.summary: Post-World War One Germany printed money to pay reparations, producing hyperinflation; the Rentenmark stabilized it. Cowrie shells served as currency for about two thousand years, mainly from the Maldives, until the mid-nineteenth century.

segments.title: Etymology of money words and simoleon
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the origins of buck, fee, dollar (from the taler), and salary (possibly from salt, an unverified story), and the cartoon word simoleon, traced to a late nineteenth-century blend.

segments.title: Listener mail: shout-out to Bree Bagnal
segments.summary: Jared Bagnal asks for a shout-out to his wife Bree for their one-year anniversary; the hosts read it and wish them well.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts thank listeners and point to social media, email and the website.
